1. Summary

One material is fitted per shoe to its Instron foam sweep: a two-term Hyperfoam (Ogden-Hill) equilibrium network with one Maxwell branch, 6 parameters. Every sweep trace is replayed through the GPU column bed with the new two-face column contact law (ColumnBed): each midsole column has a top pressed by the last and a bottom that lands on the platen. The fit uses train cycles only; validate and repeat traces are scored, not fitted.

2. Data

Each shoe was cycled on the Instron with a full-foot last at a 0.5 s period. The programmed grid is 4 stance times (160, 200, 240, 280 ms) x 6 peak forces (800 to 2800 N in 400 N steps), 100 cycles per condition. Each condition gives two phase-averaged traces (501 samples per cycle):

  • train: mean of cycles 90-98, used by the fit;
  • validate: mean of cycles 99-100, only scored.

The programmed 320 ms block is in fact a second copy of the 200 ms block (same loaded duration). It is not a new stance time; it is used as a repeatability check (the "repeat" traces).

3. Shoe and last

The last pose over the midsole column grid comes from registration.register_last, run inside the fit. Inputs are the shoe_prep left/column_grid.npz files (canonical frame, heel at -x). The preload contact uses a linear column modulus of 3 x the initial equilibrium shear modulus; it only sets the 20 N preload estimate, and the rest pitch changes by less than 0.3 deg when it is halved or doubled.

Method

  • Last up = normal of the square attachment plate. It agrees with the stud axis to 0.002 deg. It is 3.3 deg off the STL +y axis, so last pitch and roll are fixed by the attachment and never fitted.
  • Last heel = the narrow end (23 mm narrower). The ball tread (lowest plantar point) sits at 70% of the length. The heel seat is 5.1 mm above the ball tread.
  • Shoe heel = the thicker and narrower end (canonical_frame).
  • The midsole rocks on the platen. Its pitch and roll minimize the potential energy of the 20 N preload on linear columns. A rocker sole tips until the last contact is balanced over its platen contact.
  • Last x, y and yaw minimize the soft-L1 spread of the last-to-top clearance. The last tread (surface within 45 deg of horizontal) must stay inside the midsole outline. z is set at first contact.

Caveats

  • FR3: the last tread just fits the narrow FR3 waist. The outline sets x, y and yaw, not the surface fit.
  • First contact is at the heel cup rim and heel. The forefoot footbed sits 5-9 mm below the last plantar surface.
  • The last side (left) comes from the file name. Mirror check: the left last does not fit inside the right FR3 outline at all, and fits the right Deviate worse (spread 0.88 vs 0.76 mm). The Deviate grid side cue is weak ('unverified'). shoe_prep says both scans are right shoes, so left = mirror.
  • The midsole is rigid while it rocks. The preload uses linear columns.

Legacy manifest pose (manifest_v2.json fullfoot_last), for comparison with older results

  • geometry.load_mesh reorders the STL axes to (z, y, x). This is a mirror (det -1): the left last became a right last. The legacy obj is a right shoe, so the pair still had matching sides.
  • rotation_deg [90, 0, 0] makes up = STL +y. That is 3.3 deg off the plate normal. crop_height_m 0.08 removes the stud and plate. Then pose_rotation_deg [-1.0, -1.8, 0] makes the error 5.3 deg. The load axis in the shoe frame was about 4.7 deg pitch, toe down, plus 2.5 deg roll. That pitch matches the FR3 rocker rest pitch in the table above.
  • Heel ends were on the same side. The last heel sat about 27 mm in from the midsole heel edge, at y = -6 mm. This came from bounding-box centering, not from heel alignment.
  • The 95th-percentile contact offset started 31 of 611 columns compressed by up to 1.4 mm.

4. Contact law: two-face columns

The midsole is a grid of vertical columns (about 6 mm spacing). Each column has rest thickness L, footprint area A, and two unknowns: the downward displacement of its top, t, and of its bottom, b. The compression is c = t - b. The last presses the tops; the platen supports the bottoms. Both contacts are one-way.

compression            c = t - b,     0 <= c < L
last on the top        t >= d - g     (d = last stroke, g = rest gap; the last pushes, never pulls)
platen on the bottom   b <= h         (h = rest clearance of the bottom over the platen)
outside the last       top free

energy   E = sum_i A_i W(c_i)  +  1/2 sum_faces k_ij [ (t_i - t_j)^2 + (b_i - b_j)^2 ]
         W'(c) = p(c/L): two-term Hyperfoam equilibrium pressure + Maxwell overstress
         k_ij  = mu_eq (L_i + L_j) / 2,    mu_eq = (G1 + G2) f_eq     (Pasternak shear layer, no new parameter)

reactions   T_i = last on top i (held tops only),   R_i = platen on bottom i (landed bottoms only)
balance     sum_i T_i = sum_i R_i   (the shear terms cancel over the bed)

No cross term. The energy has one shear layer at the tops and one at the bottoms, and nothing that couples a top difference to a bottom difference. An earlier variant had such a cross term. It lifted thick edge columns off the platen, so it was dropped.

Four column states (for columns under the last tread):

  • held, landed: the last presses the top and the bottom stands on the platen; the foam carries the load straight through.
  • held, floating: the last presses the top, the bottom is in the air; the column passes its load sideways to neighbours through the bottom shear layer.
  • open, landed: the bottom stands on the platen, the last does not touch the top; it carries only the shear its neighbours put on it.
  • open, floating: neither face touches; the column only follows its neighbours.

Columns outside the last tread have a free top and are only landed or floating.

Range of shear support. A held column with a floating bottom is supported only by shear from landed neighbours. In the continuum limit the bottom-layer stiffness per area is mu_eq L and the foam stiffness per area is E/L with E = 2 mu_eq at small strain, so the support decays over a length lambda = sqrt(mu_eq L^2 / E) = L/sqrt(2), about 14-25 mm for 20-35 mm thick columns, and less once the foam stiffens at large strain. A floating region much wider than that gets almost no support.

Solver. One CUDA block per world runs red-black Gauss-Seidel sweeps. Each column update solves its local 2x2 problem exactly over the active constraints. A step limiter (fraction-to-boundary, factor 0.5) lets one update close at most half of the remaining open thickness L - c, so a far-off step cannot jump into the foam lock-up near c = L. Converged states are not changed by it.

Physical checks. A replayed cycle counts as physical only if T and R are finite, the platen only pushes, and |sum T - sum R| stays within 2% of the peak load every frame (last_replay.physical). A cycle that fails returns NaN. In the fit, a start whose own replay is not physical stops with a message, a Jacobian column is differenced from the other side, and the final scoring raises instead of writing a result. So a broken solve fails loudly instead of giving a smooth wrong force.

Old single-face law. The old bed had one unknown per column: its compression, set by the last's position, with the bottom fixed. A column whose bottom floats above the platen (arch, rocker toe and heel) cannot be described. It either carried nothing (old law, option A) or it was treated as standing on the platen and was crushed by the stroke plus its clearance (the "grounded columns" stopgap). The new law lets the bottom land when it reaches the platen, so floating columns carry load only once they really touch.

5. Results per shoe

Train loss is the mean squared residual of core.force_residual (force over the cycle, loop area x5, peak x6, all relative). Each start is a bounded least-squares solve with up to 80 residual evaluations; all starts run together on the GPU. Cells marked red miss at least one 10% gate (peak, RMSE, loading or unloading RMSE, loop area).

G1, G2 and alpha2 trade off between near-best starts, but the derived mu_eq, f_eq and tau stay tight. The second Hyperfoam term acts as a densification wall whose onset is identified and whose steepness is not; see the second-term section below.

Both shoes

Second Hyperfoam term: a densification wall

The second Hyperfoam term is not switched off. With alpha2 strongly negative, term2 = 2 G2 / (|alpha2| lam) (lam^-|alpha2| - 1) explodes as the stretch lam = 1 - c/L goes to 0, so a tiny G2 still gives a densification wall. The table gives term2 / term1 (the ratio is the same for the instantaneous and the equilibrium network). The wall is active when the most compressed column passes the onset strain.

ShoeG2 [Pa]alpha2term 2 / term 1 at strainWall onset strainMax column strainOnset, bound-20 fitOnset, near-best wall starts
FR30.0207-15.20.06 at 0.60, 0.47 at 0.65, 4.84 at 0.700.610.740.610.61-0.61 (n = 1)
Dev3Elite0.733-20.0 (at bound)0.03 at 0.40, 0.18 at 0.45, 1.20 at 0.50, 9.90 at 0.550.430.560.430.41-0.43 (n = 3)

The onset strain (term 2 = 10% of term 1) is the same in the bound-20 and bound-40 fits and across the near-best starts with a wall. So the wall onset is identified by this sweep; its steepness (the split between G2 and alpha2) is not. Dev3Elite pushes alpha2 to its -20 bound: it wants an even steeper wall, close to a hard stop near 0.5 strain.

Bound 20 vs bound 40

The first fit capped the term-1 exponent alpha1 at 20, and FR3 ended on that cap. The current fit allows alpha1 up to 40. The bound-20 results are from a backup and predate the kernel step-limiter fix; their Dev3Elite 280 ms / 2800 N validate score was a solver blow-up. Validate numbers: median / max over 24 traces.

7. Kernel performance

The column-bed kernel was restructured for speed with the same arithmetic per column and compiled with fast_math. Numbers from DigitalInstron/FoamSweep/fit/kernel_profile.json.

  • gpu: NVIDIA RTX A4000 Laptop GPU (sm_86, 40 SMs), Warp 1.18.0; laptop clocks drift, so before/after are interleaved in one process and minimum times are reported
  • instron_replay.setup: LastReplay.run, FR3 train traces, 24 traces x 7 candidates = 168 worlds, 917 columns, 501 frames x 2 cycles, 16 sweeps, omega 1.8
  • runner.setup: generative_runner_f01 reference scenarios; GpuBatch warm wall per step (min of 3), host simulate() per step

Where the time goes and what was tried

  • Cause of the old cost: Warp unrolled the constant row (4) and color (2) loops, so the column solve was compiled 8 times (1.16 MB cubin, 33 s cold compile) and the per-row register vectors spilled 760 B/thread to local memory.
  • Change: the bed state (top, bottom, clearance, overstress, support) lives only in shared memory and the row/half-sweep loops have runtime bounds, so the solve is compiled once with no spills; same arithmetic per column.
  • Change: a sweep that moves no column ends the step's sweeps early (block-wide flag); the next sweep would reproduce the same state, so this is bitwise neutral (verified) and helps the runner in flight (64x16: about 12%), not the Instron replay (never exactly at a fixed point).
  • Forces change by at most 5.9e-6 of the peak (Instron) and 0.0065 N (runner GRF) versus the old build. This is compiler rounding (FMA contraction differs between the unrolled and the single copy), amplified by the unconverged 16-sweep solve; changing only the block-reduction order (512 lanes) already moves forces by 2.4e-7, and 16 sweeps differ from a converged solve by about 1.5e-4. Bitwise identity with the old build is not reachable by any restructuring.
  • Where the time goes now (attribution by removing parts): the 16 sweeps are about 86% of a step; inside a column update the active-set solve is about 42% and the two Hyperfoam pressure evaluations (4 powf) about 28% of the launch. The kernel is latency-bound: 2 blocks of 256 lanes per SM (16 warps, 33% occupancy, register-limited at 128).
  • Host side: the Instron cycle is one CUDA graph; graph and eager replays take the same time and host launch cost is ~24 us against ~0.8 ms of GPU work per step, so host work is not a bottleneck.
  • Tried, not kept: precomputed face couplings in shared memory (11% slower); launch_bounds (256,3)/(256,4) (register caps 80/64 spill, 15-60% slower); launch_bounds (256,1) (30% slower); 128 or 512 lanes per world (2-30% slower); two columns per lane for ILP (8% slower); enable_backward=False (no runtime change).
  • Adopted fast_math after the accuracy study (result_changing_study): it adds 3e-6 of peak against the converged solve, the 16-sweep truncation error is 5.8e-3 (FR3) / 2.3e-3 (Dev3). The convergence-tolerance exit was not adopted.
  • Per-kernel 'after' times are scaled from a separate profiling process to the interleaved launch time (clock drift between processes).

fast_math is on: against a converged solve it changes forces by about 3e-6 of the peak, far below the 16-sweep truncation error. A convergence-based early exit from the sweeps was studied and not adopted (result_changing_study).

8. Open issues

  • Hysteresis at low force. The loop area is the largest error, worst at 800 N (FR3 34.8-42.3%, Dev3Elite 33.0-35.2%). One Maxwell branch with one relaxation time does not shape the small loops well.
  • Load outside the last. Columns that the last never touches still carry FR3 24.1-38.4%, Dev3Elite 29.3-30.7% of the platen load at peak through shear. This share is not measured; a pressure-mat test would check it.
  • Parameters at a bound. FR3: alpha1 = 23.14 (upper bound 40); no other parameter at a bound; Dev3Elite: alpha1 = 9.40 (upper bound 40); at a bound: alpha2. Dev3Elite drives alpha2 to its lower bound: it wants a steeper densification wall, close to a hard stop near 0.5 strain. G2 is tiny on purpose (it sets the wall steepness together with alpha2) and is not listed.
  • Shoe and last side. The left last is assumed from the STL file name; the side is not confirmed.
  • Runner migration. The GPU runner already steps the same ColumnBed kernel with the fitted shoes, but its gait results are not yet validated against measured references.

9. How to reproduce

PowerShell, from the repository root. Split the raw sweeps, fit each shoe, build this report, open the interactive viewer. Each fit starts from the calibrated material, the two earlier fits in DigitalInstron/FoamSweep/fit/history, and six Latin-hypercube starts (seed 0). See DigitalInstron/FoamSweep/README.md for the data files.

git lfs pull
uv run --extra dev python -m projects.digital_instron_v2.sweep_split
uv run --extra dev -m projects.digital_instron_v2 fit --shoe DigitalInstron/puma-fast-r-nitro-elite-3 --sweep DigitalInstron/FoamSweep/processed/FR3 --out DigitalInstron/FoamSweep/fit/puma-fast-r-nitro-elite-3 --start DigitalInstron/FoamSweep/fit/history/puma-fast-r-nitro-elite-3_C2nx/material_fit.json --start DigitalInstron/FoamSweep/fit/history/puma-deviate-nitro-elite-3_C2nx/material_fit.json
uv run --extra dev -m projects.digital_instron_v2 fit --shoe DigitalInstron/puma-deviate-nitro-elite-3 --sweep DigitalInstron/FoamSweep/processed/Dev3Elite --out DigitalInstron/FoamSweep/fit/puma-deviate-nitro-elite-3 --start DigitalInstron/FoamSweep/fit/history/puma-fast-r-nitro-elite-3_C2nx/material_fit.json --start DigitalInstron/FoamSweep/fit/history/puma-deviate-nitro-elite-3_C2nx/material_fit.json
uv run --extra dev python -m projects.digital_instron_v2.sweep_report --out DigitalInstron/FoamSweep/fit/report.html
uv run --extra dev -m projects.digital_instron_v2.example --shoe DigitalInstron/puma-fast-r-nitro-elite-3 --shoe DigitalInstron/puma-deviate-nitro-elite-3 --slow-motion 6.7
